newsitem.title: GERMANY: German stocks extend losses after U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: German stocks extend losses after U.S. data.

text.p: German shares on Tuesday reversed most of the gains made the previous day, with dealers saying the overnight retreat of the dollar and weakness on Wall Street were dampening sentiment.
"We have lost what we gained yesterday, but volumes are relatively weak. Most players have had enough and just want to celebrate Christmas," said one dealer.
The DAX-30 index of 30 top German shares closed 40.66 points, or 1.42 percent, lower at 2,815.13, wiping out most of the 56-point gain made on Monday.
The index slipped lower after the bourse close following stronger-than-expected U.S. November housing starts data, sparking interest rate worries in global markets.
The IBIS DAX, measuring all-day electronic dealings in the DAX, later ended at 2,808.50 points, down 32.66 points, earlier touching a day's low of 2,795.32.
But dealers said the crucial 2,800 point mark should hold this week. "We've had a terrific year and we don't want to ruin that in the last two weeks of the year," said one.

The dollar had on Monday firmed on the perception that the monetary union stability pact reached by European finance ministers in Dublin on Friday made Europe's planned currency union all the more likely, thus reducing the power of the mark.

But overnight the U.S. currency slipped more than 1/2 a pfennig to around 1.545 marks on worries ahead of Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, although most analysts expected no change in U.S. interest rates.
The dollar's weakness weighed particularly on export-oriented stocks such as chemicals companies BASF AG, Hoechst AG and Bayer AG.

Meanwhile, Commerzbank, Germany's third largest bank, was one of the few large stocks to buck the downward trend, up 34 pfennigs at 38.44 marks in IBIS dealings on a resurgence of takeover speculation in the banking sector, although the bank said it had no comment to make on such rumours.
In mid-November Commerzbank had already surged on rumours a single large investor was buying up its shares, talk the bank moved to quash.
German software firm SAP AG registered the only other significant movement, with its ordinary shares slipping nearly four percent or eight marks to 200 marks.
Dealers said news that board member Hans Werner Hector was resigning from the board of directors was hurting the stock.
